overview: Achumawi names related communities of the Pit River region in northeastern California. It is also associated more narrowly with the Ajumawi band around Fall River. Local communities historically governed themselves and maintained relationships through language and marriage; the regional label should not erase their differences.

periods.title: River-centred communities
periods.summary: The regional archaeological synthesis describes continued reliance on river resources during this period. Changes in projectile-point styles help organise the sequence, without dating the founding of a people.

periods.title: Settlement, dispossession and return
periods.summary: Settler expansion brought violence, disease and forced removal to Round Valley. Achumawi and Atsugewi people later returned to their homelands. These losses did not end community life.

periods.title: The Pit River Tribe’s written constitution
periods.summary: The wider Pit River Tribe adopted a written constitution in 1964. Its autonomous bands include Ajumawi, Atsugewi and other communities, linked within a common political body.

items.text: At Ahjumawi Lava Springs, rock walls around cold-water springs direct Sacramento sucker fish into enclosures. Openings can be closed during the catch and reopened afterwards. Crystal Spring preserves a particularly elaborate arrangement of channels and chambers, linking the design to fish behaviour and flowing water.

Inner walls expose gravel to spring water, where suckers deposit eggs. Foster interprets this layout, regular clearing and Indigenous explanations of maintenance as fishery management as well as capture. The interpretation rests on several kinds of evidence; the walls alone would not reveal all the builders’ intentions.

Foster observed Floyd Buckskin’s fishing at Ja-She Creek. The account describes an Elder directing the catch and reopening the trap after sufficient fish were taken. Fish were dried or smoked, shared with relatives and sometimes exchanged for venison or acorns, carrying the harvest into later meals.

Tule blinders collected in 1902 protected fishers’ eyes from glare during night spearing. Barter describes a braided headband and woven panels, but notes their unworn condition: they may have been made for Hudson’s collection. They preserve manufacturing knowledge without proving that this particular pair was used.

A surviving fishing net uses fine, twisted Apocynum plant-fibre cord. Two differently coloured closing cords may have helped orient it in moving water. Barter distinguishes that proposed use from the net’s observable construction and also notes discrepancies between older equipment labels.

The collected fishhooks combine a bone barb, a wooden shank and fine binding, with each hook attached to its own line. Barter could inspect the parts but could not establish exactly how the stored set was arranged for fishing. The surviving object leaves that practical detail unresolved.

UC Davis holds an Achumawi seed beater, catalogued as CHM 22, in Merriam’s basketry collection. The implement broadens the material record beyond fishing to gathering plant foods. The collection includes used household objects and notes about their uses; its general collecting dates do not precisely date this particular piece.

The regional account describes partly underground winter homes and lighter summer shelters of brush or tule matting. Fish, waterfowl, acorns and other seasonal foods supported settlements near streams and wetlands. Household life depended on several linked habitats, rather than fishing alone.

Much of the Fall River homeland passed into power-company and ranch ownership. California State Parks acquired the present park land in 1975. Protecting a park landscape is therefore one recent chapter in a much longer Indigenous history, not the beginning of its cultural importance.

In 1986 and 1987, the Pit River Tribal Council and California State Parks collaborated to protect the fish traps. The structures remained connected to people with practical knowledge and responsibilities, rather than being only abandoned features for outside researchers to interpret.

The Tribe’s constitution identifies autonomous bands within a common political body and makes protection of land, resources, culture and descendants explicit purposes. Its 1964 adoption records a modern institution exercising community responsibilities; it is not a claim that Pit River peoples first existed in that year.

ending.text: Achumawi communities continue within the wider Pit River Tribe. Colonial dispossession did not erase their identity, and the Tribe maintains institutions for land, culture and community welfare. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint is not an extinction or conquest date.
